beliefs.practice: Use a stable customerId as the document _id (or as the partition key + unique id) and perform upserts by _id to ensure idempotent merges: db.collection.updateOne({_id: customerId}, {$set: {...}}, {upsert: true}).
Choose the partition key to be customerId (or another high-cardinality stable id) so each customer profile is co-located in one partition and single-document operations avoid cross-partition costs.

Configure Mongoose/Mongo driver connection pooling and set sensible timeouts: use unifiedTopology: true, useNewUrlParser: true, maxPoolSize (e.g., 50), serverSelectionTimeoutMS and socketTimeoutMS to avoid hung connections on cloud clusters.

Never commit the connection string or primary keys to source control: read DOCUMENTDB_URI (and any credentials) from environment variables or a secret store (Azure Key Vault) and provide an .env.example with placeholders only.
Use update operators ($set, $setOnInsert, $inc) and dot notation to merge source-specific nested sub-documents instead of replacing full documents (e.g., $set: { 'sources.crm': mergedFields }).
Create an index on customerId (or _id) and any frequently queried nested attributes (e.g., sources.crm.email) ahead of time via migration scripts rather than creating indexes ad-hoc at runtime.

For vector search: store normalized embedding arrays in a dedicated field (e.g., embedding.vector) with a consistent fixed dimension and create the cluster's vector index (HNSW/IVF) with matching dimension and metric before running similarity queries.
Handle rate limiting (HTTP 429 / RU throttling) and transient network errors by implementing exponential backoff and respecting Retry-After headers; avoid tight retry loops that amplify load.

Monitor RU/s consumption, request charge per query, index usage and latency with Azure Monitor/metrics and instrument the app to log requestCharge to detect expensive operations and tune indexes or queries accordingly.
Avoid indexing very large or frequently-updated sub-doc arrays; instead, index only the fields used in filters/sorts. Remove wildcard indexing on entire documents unless necessary to reduce RU costs.

Provision throughput according to expected traffic and consider autoscale or database-level (shared) throughput for dev/test; ensure RU provisioning matches the seed/load script to avoid 429s during seeding.

Use TLS/SSL for all connections and enable firewall/VNet restrictions, IP allowlists and least-privilege database users; do not use admin keys for application runtime if role-based access or scoped secondary users are available.

Keep upsert operations as single-document updates (no multi-document transactions) for performance; if you must perform multi-document atomic changes, consider transactions but only when supported and necessary.

Use optimistic concurrency where appropriate: read _etag (Cosmos) or check a lastModified field to detect concurrent writes and avoid lost updates when multiple sources update the same profile concurrently.

Write integration/seed scripts and tests to target a dedicated database name (sample_customer_360_01 here) and to clean up test data after runs; make DB name configurable via env var to avoid accidental cross-database changes.

Create collection/container-level unique constraints for customer identity if you need DB-enforced uniqueness (Cosmos uses uniqueKey policy; Mongo API supports unique indexes) rather than relying on application logic alone.

Avoid large documents that exceed the service document size limits (e.g., 2MB/16MB depending on API); keep customer profile documents reasonably small or split rarely-used large blobs into separate storage.
Create indexes for sorting queries you run (e.g., lastUpdated) and prefer range-based pagination (filter by lastUpdated > lastSeen) over skip/limit for large collections to reduce RU cost.

Perform schema validation in the application layer (Mongoose schemas/validators) and optionally enable server-side validation where supported to avoid corrupt/invalid profiles; keep schema migrations scripted and repeatable.

Create indexes and any vector index using the cluster's management tools or migration scripts (not on every app start); verify index creation and query plans with the cluster's tools (MCP/portal) before running production traffic.
